1-1.text: Part one. What is power? ... Every electrical device has a power. Power tells you how fast a device transfers energy.

1-2.text: Power is measured in watts, written W. 1 watt means 1 joule of energy is transferred every second.

1-3.text: A 10 watt LED bulb transfers 10 joules every second. A 60 watt bulb transfers 60 joules every second, so it uses energy six times as fast.

1-4.text: Big powers are written in kilowatts. Kilo means a thousand, so 1 kilowatt equals 1000 watts. A 2000 watt kettle is a 2 kilowatt kettle.

2-1.text: Part two. Energy equals power times time. ... To work out the energy transferred: energy equals power times time. Power in watts, times time in seconds, gives energy in joules.

2-2.text: A 40 watt lamp is on for 10 seconds. Energy equals 40 times 10, which is 400 joules.

2-3.text: The time must be in seconds. A 10 watt lamp is on for 2 minutes. 2 minutes is 120 seconds, so energy equals 10 times 120, which is 1200 joules.

2-4.text: You can go the other way too: power equals energy divided by time. A hairdryer transfers 12,000 joules in 10 seconds. Power equals 12,000 divided by 10, which is 1200 watts.

3-1.text: Part three. Kilowatt-hours. ... A home uses millions of joules every day. So energy companies use a much bigger unit of energy: the kilowatt-hour.

3-2.text: 1 kilowatt-hour is the energy a 1 kilowatt device transfers in 1 hour. That is 3.6 million joules!

3-3.text: Energy in kilowatt-hours equals power in kilowatts times time in hours. A 2 kilowatt heater on for 4 hours uses 2 times 4, which is 8 kilowatt-hours.

3-4.text: Change watts to kilowatts first. A 200 watt TV is 0.2 kilowatts. On for 5 hours, it uses 0.2 times 5, which is 1 kilowatt-hour.

4-1.text: Part four. Paying for energy. ... You pay for every kilowatt-hour you use. In our examples, electricity costs 25 pence for each kilowatt-hour.

4-2.text: Cost equals energy in kilowatt-hours times the price per kilowatt-hour. The heater used 8 kilowatt-hours. 8 times 25 pence is 200 pence, which is 2 pounds.

4-3.text: An electricity meter counts the kilowatt-hours a home uses. On Monday it reads 5120. On Friday it reads 5150. 5150 minus 5120 is 30 kilowatt-hours used.

4-4.text: So the cost from Monday to Friday is 30 times 25 pence, which is 750 pence, or 7 pounds 50.

5-1.text: Part five. Comparing and saving. ... How much energy a device uses depends on two things: its power and how long it is on.

5-2.text: A 2 kilowatt hairdryer on for 15 minutes, which is a quarter of an hour, uses 2 times 0.25, which is 0.5 kilowatt-hours. A 100 watt TV on for 5 hours uses 0.1 times 5, which is 0.5 kilowatt-hours. Exactly the same!

5-3.text: Ways to save energy: switch off lights and screens, use LED bulbs, have shorter showers, and turn the heating down a little.

5-4.text: Saving energy saves money. It can also mean less fuel is burned in power stations, which is better for the planet.
